rationale: This historical paper examines the response of medical, political (unreformed Poor Law overseers/guardians and Board of Health) and religious authorities to the 1832 cholera epidemic in Birmingham, focusing on epidemic mortality and popular disturbances over swift corpse removal. Although it notes in passing that deep artesian wells supplied most drinking water (before waterborne cholera transmission was recognized in 1854), it does not study household/community water or sanitation service access, legal/administrative rules governing service access or any water/sanitation access outcome (E01).
plain_vs_narrow_note: Excluded under both narrow and plain readings because the paper is a historical historiography study of medical, Poor Law and religious responses to the 1832 cholera outbreak and corpse removal in Birmingham rather than water or sanitation service access.

evidence_quotes.quote: This paper intends to explore the response of the medical, political, and religious authorities of Birmingham to the outbreak of cholera in 1832 as well as the popular reaction to this response.
Here, swift removal of corpses clashed with traditional funeral practices and the widespread fear of "burking" by anatomists provoked serious disturbances.
